chapterTitle: Abstract Classes and Interfaces for Game Systems
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute mixed video lesson. Start with a conceptual explanation of abstract classes versus interfaces using clear diagrams (e.g., a `Shape` abstract class vs. an `IDrawable` interface, then extend to game examples like `ABaseEnemy` vs. `IInteractable`). Then, transition to a live coding demo in Unreal Engine. Show the creation of a `UInterface` (`ICollectable`) with a `BlueprintNativeEvent` function (`OnCollected`). Demonstrate its implementation in two different `AActor` classes (`ACoin` and `AHealthPotion`), providing distinct C++ `_Implementation` logic for each. Finally, show a player character C++ class that uses a line trace to find `ICollectable` actors and calls `ICollectable::Execute_OnCollected()` on them polymorphically. Emphasize the `Execute_` syntax and the benefits of loose coupling. Include a challenge where the learner adds a new interface function (e.g., `OnFocusChanged`) and implements it in one of the collectable items.

screens.title: Abstract Classes and Interfaces for Game Systems
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why abstract classes and interfaces are essential when building game systems in Unreal Engine. We’ll ground the ideas in concrete C++ and engine patterns you will use every day: pure virtual functions to force derived classes to provide behavior, and UInterface-based contracts to let unrelated classes share behavior without changing their inheritance. You will see examples that include an abstract enemy base, a door that implements an interaction contract, and the correct way to call interface functions so Blueprint overrides and native implementations both work. This matters because as your project grows, tight coupling quickly becomes a maintenance problem. Using abstract classes and interfaces the right way keeps systems decoupled, makes testing and iteration easier, and lets designers extend gameplay in Blueprints without editing core C++ hierarchies. Listen for concrete code patterns such as the I-prefixed C++ interface, the BlueprintNativeEvent with an _Implementation method, and the Execute_ call that routes through Unreal’s reflection. By the end you’ll know when to use an abstract base type and when to reach for a UInterface contract, and you’ll be ready to implement interaction systems that are robust and extendable.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use abstract classes for shared base behavior; use UInterface when you need multiple, independent behavior contracts across unrelated classes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Overview

Abstract Classes & UInterface Patterns

Build common behaviors or define loose contracts so multiple actors can share capabilities without rigid inheritance.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Define abstract classes. Implement UInterface. Call interface methods safely with Execute_.
Coming up
Hands-on example: A door and a pickup item that both implement an interactable contract.
Why it matters
Loose coupling lets you change internals without touching callers and enables Blueprints to override behavior safely.
Common pitfall
Calling interface methods directly instead of via Execute_ will bypass Blueprint overrides.
Explore Key Topics
Abstract Class
Defines pure virtual functions so derived types must implement behavior.
UInterface
Engine-level contract allowing many classes to implement the same API.
Execute_
Use this prefix to ensure correct dispatch to C++ or Blueprint implementations.
Concept snapshot
Abstract base vs. interface — balance shared code and flexible contracts.
Try thinking about whether your behavior is an "is-a" relationship with common data, or a "can-do" capability that many unrelated actors need to share.
Quick example
An ABaseEnemy abstract class forces AttackBehavior to exist. A Door implements IInteractable to allow players to open it regardless of its actor type.
Key takeaway
Mix both patterns: share implementation with abstract bases, and share capabilities with interfaces.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will understand both the conceptual differences and the concrete C++ patterns for abstract classes and Unreal interfaces. First, you will be able to define and implement an abstract class with pure virtual functions so derived actors must provide behavior. Second, you will declare and implement a UInterface so any UCLASS can pick up a capability regardless of its inheritance. Third, you will recognize when to choose an abstract class versus an interface based on whether you need a shared base or a flexible capability. Finally, you will reliably call interface functions using the engine-safe Execute_ syntax and check Implements<> to avoid runtime errors. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a milestone you can verify in your project: compiling an abstract base, implementing an interface on two actors, and wiring an interaction call that triggers a Blueprint override. These skills are practical: they let designers work in Blueprints while engineers keep core systems in C++, and they reduce coupling in large projects. We'll practice these steps with examples and an interaction demo so you can test each milestone quickly.

Learning Objectives

Learn → Understand → Apply → Master

screens.title: Practical Skills & Milestones
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide lists hands-on milestones you’ll perform during the guided lab. You will create a UInterface and mark it Blueprintable so designers can implement behavior in Blueprints. You will implement that interface on at least two different actor types—one representing a door and one representing a pickup—so you practice polymorphic interaction. You will implement a BlueprintNativeEvent so you can provide a default C++ implementation and allow Blueprints to override it; the C++ side uses the _Implementation method name. Finally, you will wire your player character to perform a line trace and call the interface function only when the target actor implements the interface using the Implements template. These are testable: compile the project, place actors in the level, press your interaction key, and observe distinct logs based on each actor’s implementation. These steps reinforce loose coupling and let you iterate on gameplay without rewriting actor inheritance chains.

screens.title: What is an Abstract Class and a Pure Virtual Function?
screens.narratorSegment: An abstract class is a C++ class that cannot be instantiated because it declares at least one pure virtual function. A pure virtual function is a virtual declaration assigned to zero, which forces every concrete derived class to implement that function. The practical value in games is clear: when you have a family of related objects that share a role but implement it differently, an abstract base can guarantee a common A P I. For example, imagine ABaseEnemy defines a pure virtual AttackBehavior method. Roof and implementation details can vary between AZombie and ASpider, but both will provide AttackBehavior. This lets other code hold an ABaseEnemy pointer and call AttackBehavior safely, invoking the concrete implementation for each enemy type. A common misconception is to treat abstract classes like interfaces; while both enforce a contract, abstract classes can also provide shared implementation and data members. Use an abstract base when derived types should share internal state or helper methods. A mistake is to overload the base with unrelated responsibilities; keep the base focused on shared behavior for a coherent family. As a takeaway, use abstract classes to enforce 'is-a' relationships where a common foundation and shared data make sense.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Abstract classes enforce required methods via pure virtual functions and can share implementation details among related types.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Abstract Class

Abstract Class & Pure Virtual Function

Declare a method that derived classes must implement, and optionally share implementation or state in the base.

<!-- Example: ABaseEnemy -->
// ABaseEnemy.h
class ABaseEnemy
{
public:
  virtual void AttackBehavior() = 0; // pure virtual, makes class abstract
  virtual ~ABaseEnemy() = default;
};

// Derived classes must implement AttackBehavior
class AZombie : public ABaseEnemy
{
public:
  virtual void AttackBehavior() override { /* zombie-specific attack */ }
};
Explanation
  • Pure virtual functions declare required behavior but do not provide implementation.
  • Abstract classes can also hold shared data and helper methods used by derived types.
  • Treat them as the canonical "is-a" relationship in your type hierarchy.
Concrete example
ABaseEnemy requires AttackBehavior; AZombie and ASpider implement it differently so AI can call attack polymorphically.
Key Takeaway

Use abstract classes to guarantee behavior and share implementation among a related family of types.

screens.title: Polymorphism with Abstract Bases
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism is the ability to treat different concrete types through a common interface — in C++ this is often an abstract base with virtual functions. The practical outcome in games is simple: you can write AI managers, damage systems, or spawn controllers that store pointers to the abstract base and call required methods without knowing the concrete type. For example, an enemy manager can keep a list of ABaseEnemy pointers and call AttackBehavior on each. Each derived enemy implements that method differently, so the correct behavior executes at runtime. A common misconception is that polymorphism requires expensive runtime checks; in fact, C++ virtual dispatch is the designed mechanism for this pattern. However, be mindful that abstract bases create a single inheritance path. If you must add unrelated capabilities later, you risk running into the single-inheritance limitation. That leads to interfaces. A concrete example: a swarm update loop calls AttackBehavior on each ABaseEnemy; the loop doesn't care whether the object is AZombie or ASpider. For practice, implement a small concrete derived class, compile, and confirm your manager calls the concrete override via the base pointer. How does this change when a class also needs unrelated capabilities? We'll explore that next.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism
keyIdea.text: Use base-class pointers to call required behavior across a family of derived types, enabling generic managers and systems.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Polymorphism

Polymorphism in practice

A manager holds base pointers and calls required methods; each derived type implements behavior differently.

// EnemyManager.cpp (conceptual)
TArray<ABaseEnemy*> Enemies;

for (ABaseEnemy* E : Enemies)
{
  if (E) E->AttackBehavior(); // virtual dispatch calls AZombie or ASpider implementation
}
Why this matters
Systems become generic and simpler: a single loop can update many enemy types, and adding a new enemy only requires implementing the base methods.
Concrete example
AZombie overrides AttackBehavior with a staggered lunge; ASpider overrides it with a pounce. The manager calls AttackBehavior without special cases.
Key Takeaway

Polymorphism reduces branching and makes adding new creatures straightforward — until you need multiple independent capabilities, when interfaces help.

screens.title: Single Inheritance Limits and the Need for Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: C++ enforces single inheritance for base class subobjects, which means a class can only inherit directly from one concrete base. When an object needs many independent capabilities, single inheritance becomes restrictive. For example, a Door might logically be both interactable and damageable. If you modeled both behaviors as abstract bases, you'd force the door into a fragile hierarchy or resort to awkward multiple inheritance. Interfaces solve this: they describe a 'can-do' capability without imposing a single inheritance structure. In Unreal Engine, UInterface is the engine's mechanism for this pattern: declare a UINTERFACE and an I-prefixed class with the function signatures; any UCLASS can implement the I class to promise those behaviors. This creates loose coupling because other systems only need to know that an actor implements the interface, not its position in an inheritance tree. A common misconception is thinking interfaces provide shared implementation; in Unreal, interfaces are contracts. If you need shared helper code, combine a lightweight base class for shared code and interfaces for orthogonal capabilities, or prefer composition. The takeaway: prefer abstract base classes for tight family relationships and UInterface when you need many independent capabilities across unrelated classes.

keyIdea.title: Why interfaces
keyIdea.text: Interfaces provide flexible, orthogonal capabilities that multiple unrelated classes can implement without changing inheritance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Interfaces vs Base Classes

Single inheritance issue

If you model every capability as an abstract base, you restrict classes to a single base and lose flexibility when an object needs multiple roles.

Scenario
  • A Door should be interactable and damageable.
  • Enemies should be damageable but are unrelated to doors.
  • Interfaces let both doors and enemies implement damageable behavior without shared inheritance.

Interface advantage

Interfaces let any UCLASS implement a contract, enabling loose coupling and multiple orthogonal behaviors on the same object.

Note
Interfaces do not, by themselves, provide shared implementation. Use them to define behavior; provide shared helpers elsewhere as needed.
Concrete advice
If many unrelated types need the same capability, use a UInterface. If a family of types share data and many methods, prefer an abstract base.

screens.title: Declaring a UInterface in Unreal
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's UInterface pattern is intentionally two-part. First you declare a UINTERFACE class, which is the UObject-based reflection type that allows Unreal to expose the interface to Blueprints and the editor. Second you declare an I-prefixed C++ class that carries the actual function signatures that implementers will inherit from. The UINTERFACE is typically marked Blueprintable so designers can implement the interface in Blueprint classes, and functions use BlueprintNativeEvent if you want to provide a C++ default while still permitting Blueprint overrides. The header example in the lesson shows the UINTERFACE declaration followed by the IInteractable class with a UFUNCTION marked BlueprintCallable and BlueprintNativeEvent. This split is unusual if you come from plain C++ interfaces, but it integrates with the engine’s reflection system and ensures both C++ and Blueprint implementations can coexist. A common mistake is to forget the I prefix for the C++ class or to omit the BlueprintNativeEvent specifier when you intended to allow Blueprint overrides. Keep the two parts together, and name them clearly so implementers understand which header to include. Declaring a UInterface in Unreal means a uinterface for reflection + an i-prefixed c++ class for function signatures enables blueprintable contracts.. In practical terms, the uinterface macro and the i-prefixed c++ contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UInterface pattern
keyIdea.text: A UINTERFACE for reflection + an I-prefixed C++ class for function signatures enables Blueprintable contracts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › UInterface Declaration

Header pattern

You create a UINTERFACE class and an I-prefixed class with the function signatures and UFUNCTION specifiers.

// Interactable.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "UObject/Interface.h"
#include "Interactable.generated.h"

UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable)
class UInteractable : public UInterface
{
    GENERATED_BODY()
};

class MYPROJECT_API IInteractable
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, BlueprintNativeEvent, Category = "Interaction")
    void OnInteract(AActor* InstigatorActor);
};

Notes & common pitfalls

  • Remember the I prefix for the C++ contract class (IInteractable).
  • Use BlueprintNativeEvent if you want both a C++ default and Blueprint override.
  • Include the generated header to integrate with Unreal's reflection system.
Naming consistency and the macro calls are important to avoid confusing linking or reflection errors at compile time.

screens.title: Implementing a UInterface on a UCLASS
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing a UInterface on a UCLASS involves adding public IYourInterface to your class inheritance list and providing the implementation for the BlueprintNativeEvent function using the _Implementation suffix. For example, an AMyDoor actor inherits both from AActor and public IInteractable. In the header you declare the virtual OnInteract_Implementation method override, and in the CPP file you implement the behavior — perhaps checking a bIsLocked flag and logging the result or destroying the actor. The BlueprintNativeEvent specifier means Unreal generates a thunk that will call either the Blueprint override or the C++ _Implementation. When you implement the function in C++ name it OnInteract_Implementation. Do not call OnInteract directly on the actor; instead use the Execute_ wrapper when invoking on potentially varied actors. A common misconception is expecting the method without the suffix to be called automatically. The engine's generated Execute_ function handles routing so both C++ and Blueprint implementers respond correctly. Keep your implementations focused: the _Implementation method should contain default logic, and designers may override the behavior in Blueprints when needed. Implementing a UInterface on a UCLASS means use public iinterface in the class declaration and implement the blueprintnativeevent using the _implementation method for default c++ behavior.. In practical terms, add public iinterface and provide the _implementation method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use public IInterface in the class declaration and implement the BlueprintNativeEvent using the _Implementation method for default C++ behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › UInterface Implementation

Header example (implementer)

// MyDoor.h
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AMyDoor : public AActor, public IInteractable
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AMyDoor();

    virtual void OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor) override;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite)
    bool bIsLocked;
};

CPP example (default behavior)

// MyDoor.cpp
void AMyDoor::OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor)
{
    if (bIsLocked)
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Door is locked!"));
    }
    else
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Door opened by %s!"), *InstigatorActor->GetName());
        Destroy();
    }
}
This default implementation can be extended or replaced by a Blueprint override. Keep default logic concise and safe; designers can add polish in Blueprint without altering the C++ implementation.

screens.title: Calling Interface Functions Safely
screens.narratorSegment: When you want to call an interface function on an actor in Unreal, you must ensure the call goes through the reflection layer so Blueprint overrides are respected. The correct pattern starts with a safety check: call Implements with the UInterface type to confirm the object implements the contract. Once confirmed, call IYourInterface::Execute_Function on the instance, passing required parameters. The Execute_ wrapper makes the engine route the call to either the C++ _Implementation or the Blueprint override. A frequent mistake is attempting to call the interface function directly on the actor pointer; that bypasses the generated dispatch and may not invoke a Blueprint implementation. The chapter provides an example: after an overlap, check OtherActor->Implements<UInteractable>(), then call IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(OtherActor, this). This ensures that both Blueprints and native C++ behaviors respond correctly. As a practical tip, use the Implements check in places where the object type is not statically known, and prefer strong typing when you control both caller and callee. This pattern keeps your game flexible and prevents subtle runtime mismatches between C++ and Blueprint paths. Calling Interface Functions Safely means always check implements and call iinterface::execute_method to ensure correct dispatch to c++ or blueprint implementations.. In practical terms, use implements<> and the execute_ prefix to dispatch correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Door implementation (excerpt)

// Door.h (excerpt)
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API ADoor : public AActor, public IInteractable
{
    GENERATED_BODY()
public:
    ADoor();
    virtual void OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor) override;
    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere)
    bool bIsLocked;
};

// Door.cpp (excerpt)
void ADoor::OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor)
{
    if (bIsLocked)
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Door is locked!"));
    }
    else
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Door opened by %s!"), *InstigatorActor->GetName());
        Destroy();
    }
}

Pickup implementation (excerpt)

// PickupItem.cpp (excerpt)
void APickupItem::OnInteract_Implementation(AActor* InstigatorActor)
{
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Item collected by %s!"), *InstigatorActor->GetName());
    Destroy();
}

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Player Interaction

TryInteract implementation

void AMyPlayerCharacter::TryInteract()
{
    FVector Start = GetActorLocation();
    FVector End = Start + GetActorForwardVector() * 200.0f;

    FHitResult Hit;
    FCollisionQueryParams Params;
    Params.AddIgnoredActor(this);

    if (GetWorld()->LineTraceSingleByChannel(Hit, Start, End, ECC_Visibility, Params))
    {
        AActor* HitActor = Hit.GetActor();
        if (HitActor && HitActor->Implements<UInteractable>())
        {
            IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(HitActor, this);
        }
    }
}
Testing checklist
  • Place ADoor and APickupItem in the level.
  • Ensure player is the default pawn and TryInteract is bound to a key.
  • Walk up and press the key; confirm different log messages and destruction behavior.
Adjust trace length and collision channel to match your level geometry so the player reliably targets intended actors.

screens.title: When to Use Abstract Classes vs Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between an abstract class and an interface comes down to the relationship you need. If you have a family of related classes that should share data or helper methods, an abstract base is appropriate: it offers a common type and shared implementation. If you need independent capabilities that multiple unrelated classes may possess, prefer an interface so you avoid inheritance conflicts. For instance, use an abstract ABaseEnemy when enemies share hit points or movement code, but use IInteractable for doors, pickups, and NPCs that simply need a response to interaction. Avoid over-creating interfaces: too many tiny interfaces can fragment your design and increase cognitive overhead. Also avoid stuffing unrelated behaviors into a single interface; interfaces should group closely related contract functions. Watch for common mistakes: forgetting the I prefix, calling interface functions directly, or relying on interfaces for heavy shared implementation. If you need both shared data and multiple capabilities, combine an abstract base for shared state and interfaces for orthogonal roles, or use composition. The goal is maintainability: pick the pattern that keeps systems decoupled while minimizing unnecessary indirection.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Architecture Guidance

Choosing the right pattern

Abstract Class
Use when types share data or implementation and are part of a coherent family, such as enemies that all need health and AI state.
Interface
Use when many unrelated types need the same capability, like interactable or damageable behaviors across diverse actors.
Pitfalls to avoid
  • Calling interface methods directly instead of using Execute_.
  • Overusing interfaces for very small, single-use contracts.
  • Putting unrelated responsibilities into one base class or interface.
When in doubt, consider the change surface: if adding a new capability should not affect existing inheritance, prefer an interface. If many types will share state and helpers, prefer an abstract base.

screens.title: Extend the Interface: Add Focus and Test
screens.narratorSegment: A practical challenge is to add a small additional function to your existing interface and implement it in one of the actors. For example, add an OnFocusChanged function to IInteractable so objects can respond when the player looks at them. Declare the function in the interface header with BlueprintNativeEvent if you want a C++ default. Implement OnFocusChanged_Implementation in your pickup to, for example, show a UI hint or change the item’s visual state. Then update your player code to call Execute_OnFocusChanged when the player is looking at an actor, perhaps during the tick or when your trace hits an actor. Test that both C++ implementations and Blueprint overrides respond. This exercise reinforces safe extension: interfaces can be extended but keep changes backward compatible. If you add required pure virtual methods to an abstract base, remember that all derived classes must be updated, which is more invasive. For this reason, prefer adding optional interface methods with default implementations when you expect incremental extension. After completing the task, ask yourself whether the new method is a capability shared across many actor types or something specific to one family; that decision guides whether it belongs in an interface or an abstract base.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why abstract classes and interfaces are essential when building game systems in Unreal Engine. We’ll ground the ideas in concrete C++ and engine patterns you will use every day: pure virtual functions to force derived classes to provide behavior, and UInterface-based contracts to let unrelated classes share behavior without changing their inheritance. You will see examples that include an abstract enemy base, a door that implements an interaction contract, and the correct way to call interface functions so Blueprint overrides and native implementations both work. This matters because as your project grows, tight coupling quickly becomes a maintenance problem. Using abstract classes and interfaces the right way keeps systems decoupled, makes testing and iteration easier, and lets designers extend gameplay in Blueprints without editing core C++ hierarchies. Listen for concrete code patterns such as the I-prefixed C++ interface, the BlueprintNativeEvent with an _Implementation method, and the Execute_ call that routes through Unreal’s reflection. By the end you’ll know when to use an abstract base type and when to reach for a UInterface contract, and you’ll be ready to implement interaction systems that are robust and extendable.

By the end of this lesson you will understand both the conceptual differences and the concrete C++ patterns for abstract classes and Unreal interfaces. First, you will be able to define and implement an abstract class with pure virtual functions so derived actors must provide behavior. Second, you will declare and implement a UInterface so any UCLASS can pick up a capability regardless of its inheritance. Third, you will recognize when to choose an abstract class versus an interface based on whether you need a shared base or a flexible capability. Finally, you will reliably call interface functions using the engine-safe Execute_ syntax and check Implements<> to avoid runtime errors. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a milestone you can verify in your project: compiling an abstract base, implementing an interface on two actors, and wiring an interaction call that triggers a Blueprint override. These skills are practical: they let designers work in Blueprints while engineers keep core systems in C++, and they reduce coupling in large projects. We'll practice these steps with examples and an interaction demo so you can test each milestone quickly.

This second objectives slide lists hands-on milestones you’ll perform during the guided lab. You will create a UInterface and mark it Blueprintable so designers can implement behavior in Blueprints. You will implement that interface on at least two different actor types—one representing a door and one representing a pickup—so you practice polymorphic interaction. You will implement a BlueprintNativeEvent so you can provide a default C++ implementation and allow Blueprints to override it; the C++ side uses the _Implementation method name. Finally, you will wire your player character to perform a line trace and call the interface function only when the target actor implements the interface using the Implements template. These are testable: compile the project, place actors in the level, press your interaction key, and observe distinct logs based on each actor’s implementation. These steps reinforce loose coupling and let you iterate on gameplay without rewriting actor inheritance chains.

An abstract class is a C++ class that cannot be instantiated because it declares at least one pure virtual function. A pure virtual function is a virtual declaration assigned to zero, which forces every concrete derived class to implement that function. The practical value in games is clear: when you have a family of related objects that share a role but implement it differently, an abstract base can guarantee a common A P I. For example, imagine ABaseEnemy defines a pure virtual AttackBehavior method. Roof and implementation details can vary between AZombie and ASpider, but both will provide AttackBehavior. This lets other code hold an ABaseEnemy pointer and call AttackBehavior safely, invoking the concrete implementation for each enemy type. A common misconception is to treat abstract classes like interfaces; while both enforce a contract, abstract classes can also provide shared implementation and data members. Use an abstract base when derived types should share internal state or helper methods. A mistake is to overload the base with unrelated responsibilities; keep the base focused on shared behavior for a coherent family. As a takeaway, use abstract classes to enforce 'is-a' relationships where a common foundation and shared data make sense.

Polymorphism is the ability to treat different concrete types through a common interface — in C++ this is often an abstract base with virtual functions. The practical outcome in games is simple: you can write AI managers, damage systems, or spawn controllers that store pointers to the abstract base and call required methods without knowing the concrete type. For example, an enemy manager can keep a list of ABaseEnemy pointers and call AttackBehavior on each. Each derived enemy implements that method differently, so the correct behavior executes at runtime. A common misconception is that polymorphism requires expensive runtime checks; in fact, C++ virtual dispatch is the designed mechanism for this pattern. However, be mindful that abstract bases create a single inheritance path. If you must add unrelated capabilities later, you risk running into the single-inheritance limitation. That leads to interfaces. A concrete example: a swarm update loop calls AttackBehavior on each ABaseEnemy; the loop doesn't care whether the object is AZombie or ASpider. For practice, implement a small concrete derived class, compile, and confirm your manager calls the concrete override via the base pointer. How does this change when a class also needs unrelated capabilities? We'll explore that next.

C++ enforces single inheritance for base class subobjects, which means a class can only inherit directly from one concrete base. When an object needs many independent capabilities, single inheritance becomes restrictive. For example, a Door might logically be both interactable and damageable. If you modeled both behaviors as abstract bases, you'd force the door into a fragile hierarchy or resort to awkward multiple inheritance. Interfaces solve this: they describe a 'can-do' capability without imposing a single inheritance structure. In Unreal Engine, UInterface is the engine's mechanism for this pattern: declare a UINTERFACE and an I-prefixed class with the function signatures; any UCLASS can implement the I class to promise those behaviors. This creates loose coupling because other systems only need to know that an actor implements the interface, not its position in an inheritance tree. A common misconception is thinking interfaces provide shared implementation; in Unreal, interfaces are contracts. If you need shared helper code, combine a lightweight base class for shared code and interfaces for orthogonal capabilities, or prefer composition. The takeaway: prefer abstract base classes for tight family relationships and UInterface when you need many independent capabilities across unrelated classes.

Unreal's UInterface pattern is intentionally two-part. First you declare a UINTERFACE class, which is the UObject-based reflection type that allows Unreal to expose the interface to Blueprints and the editor. Second you declare an I-prefixed C++ class that carries the actual function signatures that implementers will inherit from. The UINTERFACE is typically marked Blueprintable so designers can implement the interface in Blueprint classes, and functions use BlueprintNativeEvent if you want to provide a C++ default while still permitting Blueprint overrides. The header example in the lesson shows the UINTERFACE declaration followed by the IInteractable class with a UFUNCTION marked BlueprintCallable and BlueprintNativeEvent. This split is unusual if you come from plain C++ interfaces, but it integrates with the engine’s reflection system and ensures both C++ and Blueprint implementations can coexist. A common mistake is to forget the I prefix for the C++ class or to omit the BlueprintNativeEvent specifier when you intended to allow Blueprint overrides. Keep the two parts together, and name them clearly so implementers understand which header to include. Declaring a UInterface in Unreal means a uinterface for reflection + an i-prefixed c++ class for function signatures enables blueprintable contracts.. In practical terms, the uinterface macro and the i-prefixed c++ contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Implementing a UInterface on a UCLASS involves adding public IYourInterface to your class inheritance list and providing the implementation for the BlueprintNativeEvent function using the _Implementation suffix. For example, an AMyDoor actor inherits both from AActor and public IInteractable. In the header you declare the virtual OnInteract_Implementation method override, and in the CPP file you implement the behavior — perhaps checking a bIsLocked flag and logging the result or destroying the actor. The BlueprintNativeEvent specifier means Unreal generates a thunk that will call either the Blueprint override or the C++ _Implementation. When you implement the function in C++ name it OnInteract_Implementation. Do not call OnInteract directly on the actor; instead use the Execute_ wrapper when invoking on potentially varied actors. A common misconception is expecting the method without the suffix to be called automatically. The engine's generated Execute_ function handles routing so both C++ and Blueprint implementers respond correctly. Keep your implementations focused: the _Implementation method should contain default logic, and designers may override the behavior in Blueprints when needed. Implementing a UInterface on a UCLASS means use public iinterface in the class declaration and implement the blueprintnativeevent using the _implementation method for default c++ behavior.. In practical terms, add public iinterface and provide the _implementation method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you want to call an interface function on an actor in Unreal, you must ensure the call goes through the reflection layer so Blueprint overrides are respected. The correct pattern starts with a safety check: call Implements with the UInterface type to confirm the object implements the contract. Once confirmed, call IYourInterface::Execute_Function on the instance, passing required parameters. The Execute_ wrapper makes the engine route the call to either the C++ _Implementation or the Blueprint override. A frequent mistake is attempting to call the interface function directly on the actor pointer; that bypasses the generated dispatch and may not invoke a Blueprint implementation. The chapter provides an example: after an overlap, check OtherActor->Implements<UInteractable>(), then call IInteractable::Execute_OnInteract(OtherActor, this). This ensures that both Blueprints and native C++ behaviors respond correctly. As a practical tip, use the Implements check in places where the object type is not statically known, and prefer strong typing when you control both caller and callee. This pattern keeps your game flexible and prevents subtle runtime mismatches between C++ and Blueprint paths. Choosing between an abstract class and an interface comes down to the relationship you need. If you have a family of related classes that should share data or helper methods, an abstract base is appropriate: it offers a common type and shared implementation. If you need independent capabilities that multiple unrelated classes may possess, prefer an interface so you avoid inheritance conflicts. For instance, use an abstract ABaseEnemy when enemies share hit points or movement code, but use IInteractable for doors, pickups, and NPCs that simply need a response to interaction. Avoid over-creating interfaces: too many tiny interfaces can fragment your design and increase cognitive overhead. Also avoid stuffing unrelated behaviors into a single interface; interfaces should group closely related contract functions. Watch for common mistakes: forgetting the I prefix, calling interface functions directly, or relying on interfaces for heavy shared implementation. If you need both shared data and multiple capabilities, combine an abstract base for shared state and interfaces for orthogonal roles, or use composition. The goal is maintainability: pick the pattern that keeps systems decoupled while minimizing unnecessary indirection.

These are the essential terms to keep in mind as you design systems. First, an Abstract Class cannot be instantiated because it includes one or more pure virtual functions; use it to provide a shared base and common implementation. Second, a Pure Virtual Function is declared with equals zero and requires derived classes to implement the function. Third, an Interface is a contract that describes what a class can do without prescribing how it does it. These distinctions help you decide whether behavior belongs in a shared base or a cross-cutting capability. Keep these short definitions handy while you refactor or design gameplay systems so you pick the most maintainable structure. Here are the remaining engine-specific concepts that will prevent common bugs. UInterface is Unreal’s reflection-aware interface pattern that consists of a UINTERFACE reflection type and an I-prefixed C++ contract. BlueprintNativeEvent lets you provide a C++ default while allowing Blueprint overrides using the _Implementation naming convention. Loose coupling describes designing systems so components interact through interfaces rather than concrete types, which simplifies changes. Finally, the Execute_ prefix is required to correctly call interface functions on UObjects so that the engine dispatches to Blueprint or C++ implementations. A frequent error is calling interface methods directly or forgetting to check Implements which can cause calls to miss Blueprint overrides or execute on objects that don’t implement the contract. Keep these engine rules in mind as you implement and call interfaces to ensure your systems behave predictably in both C++ and Blueprint contexts.
